sentences.text: The preserved pelvis of this creature measures exactly four centimeters in length.
A distinctive trait is a triangular depression located at the upper rear corner of the hip joint, covered by a ridge.
The rear blade of the ilium forms a unique T-shape, terminating in an upward expansion longer than the shaft itself.
Fossil evidence shows the bone contains internal air chambers, a condition known as camellate bone, and all vertebrae are pneumatized.
Based on its affinities, researchers assumed the animal was toothless and likely possessed a crest on its snout.
A four-year-old girl named Daisy Morris discovered the fossil remains in November 2008 at Atherfield Point on the Isle of Wight.
The discovery was authenticated by paleontologist Martin Simpson in April 2009.
The species was formally described and named in a 2013 paper published in the journal PLoS ONE.
Darren Naish, Martin Simpson, and Gareth Dyke described the type species Vectidraco daisymorrisae.
The specific name daisymorrisae honors the discoverer Daisy Morris.
The only known specimen, a holotype from the early Aptian period 124 million years ago, was found in the Chale Clay Member of the Atherfield Clay Formation.
Initially, Vectidraco was classified in a basal position within Azhdarchoidea, which would have made it one of the smallest members of that group.
A 2018 study reclassified Vectidraco as a member of the family Tapejaridae, specifically as the sister taxon to Tapejara and Europejara.
A 2020 phylogenetic analysis by David Martill and colleagues again placed Vectidraco within the family Tapejaridae.
Vectidraco lived between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago, spanning the Barremian to Aptian stages.
